source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating decode. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Runbook: first separate time-to-first-token (prefill) from inter-token decode latency. Reproduce with fixed model, tokenizer, precision, runtime, prompt/output lengths, sampling, and concurrency; warm up, then collect repeated per-request traces for p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/s, queue time, GPU utilization, memory, and errors. Mechanism: after prefill, each decode step forms a query, attends to cached prior keys/values, and appends the current position's K/V rather than rebuilding the prefix. Boundary: bandwidth is not guaranteed to be the bottleneck—short contexts, low load, kernel launches, synchronization, or scheduler overhead may dominate. Compare cache events and utilization before attributing a regression.
risks: Combining prefill and decode hides the source of latency changes.
Hardware or scheduler counters may be unavailable or misleading.
evidence_required: Matched repeated traces with separate prefill/decode timing, cache hit/eviction events, memory/utilization telemetry, latency percentiles, and failure counts.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating decode. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Runbook: confirm that the observed metric is decode-only, then record model/runtime versions, precision, prompt and output lengths, batch/concurrency policy, and request mix. Trace one request from prefill through generation and inspect cache allocation, reuse, and eviction; repeat under controlled load. Mechanism: the next-token query reads the accumulated K/V cache and appends a new K/V entry, so the prefix need not be recomputed when reuse is supported. Boundary: cache reuse can fail or become paging/eviction overhead when prefixes, positions, attention features, or residency are incompatible. Report successful and failed requests separately with TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, memory, and tail latency.
risks: A cache miss or fallback path can be mistaken for ordinary decode behavior.
Uncontrolled request mix confounds runtime and hardware comparisons.
evidence_required: Versioned configuration, per-request traces, cache compatibility/hit/miss/eviction logs, memory telemetry, and percentile latency including failures.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating decode. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Runbook: establish a single-request warm baseline, then sweep context length, output length, and concurrency one factor at a time while keeping weights, precision, kernels, tokenizer, sampling, and stopping rules fixed. Mechanism: autoregressive decode uses the current hidden state/query to attend to stored keys and values and appends the new token's K/V; cache size therefore grows with generated context. Boundary: a speedup or bottleneck observed at one length/load point does not generalize across batching, paging, cache capacity, or scheduler regimes. Capture TTFT separately, inter-token and end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput/goodput, queue time, memory, utilization, cache events, output checks, and OOM/errors.
risks: Length and load interactions can create nonlinear capacity failures.
Latency-only comparisons can miss output or correctness regressions.
evidence_required: Raw repeated results over a length-by-load matrix, cache/memory telemetry, output validation, tail latency, and complete OOM/error accounting.

source_user: Define continuous batching and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Continuous batching is a serving policy that changes the active request set between decode iterations: completed sequences are retired and waiting requests can be admitted without waiting for every request in a static batch to finish. Mechanism: the scheduler forms each iteration from currently active requests, allowing compute slots to be reused as sequences complete; this can improve utilization and throughput for variable-length traffic. Boundary: admission, padding, memory limits, and scheduler policy still constrain behavior, and higher throughput may increase queue or tail latency. Measure per-request TTFT, inter-token/end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, queue time, tokens/s, batch occupancy, memory, and failures under a fixed arrival process.
risks: Aggregate throughput can conceal queueing or tail-latency regressions.
Benefits depend on request-length variability and scheduler implementation.
evidence_required: Batch/admission traces and per-request latency, queueing, throughput, occupancy, memory, and error metrics across controlled loads.

source_user: Define continuous batching and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Continuous batching keeps decoding a changing set of requests rather than holding a fixed batch until its longest sequence ends. At iteration boundaries, completed requests leave and eligible queued requests enter. Mechanism: this reduces idle slots caused by unequal output lengths and can keep matrix work populated, potentially raising utilization and throughput. Boundary: it is not automatically faster; admission limits, KV-cache memory, synchronization, and queueing can dominate, especially for short or low-concurrency workloads. Compare against a clearly defined static-batch baseline with identical model/runtime settings and report throughput together with TTFT, inter-token latency, tail latency, queue time, memory, and errors.
risks: A static baseline with different padding or kernels is not a causal comparison.
Improved utilization may trade against fairness and tail latency.
evidence_required: Matched baseline configuration, scheduler/admission traces, request-level latency percentiles, throughput, memory, utilization, and failure counts.

source_user: Define continuous batching and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Continuous batching is dynamic batching for iterative generation: the scheduler can retire a finished sequence and admit a waiting request at a decode iteration boundary while other requests continue. Mechanism: active requests share an iteration's kernels, but the active set is refreshed instead of being fixed for the longest sequence, reducing idle capacity from length skew. Boundary: requests must satisfy admission and KV-memory constraints; frequent churn, synchronization, or an unsuitable scheduler may erase the benefit. Validate with a representative length distribution and fixed arrival process, and record batch membership, queue time, per-request latency percentiles, throughput/goodput, memory, utilization, and failures.
risks: Synthetic equal-length traffic may hide the main batching benefit.
Admission churn can add overhead not visible in aggregate tokens/s.
evidence_required: Iteration-level batch membership/admission traces and repeated load tests with length mix, queueing, latency tails, utilization, memory, and errors.

source_user: Define continuous batching and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Continuous batching dynamically changes the decode batch at safe iteration boundaries: completed sequences are removed and waiting sequences may be inserted. Mechanism: the scheduler reuses a freed active slot for another request, limiting idle work when output lengths differ and often improving utilization. Boundary: the policy does not remove KV-cache memory, scheduling overhead, or admission limits; under memory pressure it may reject, defer, page, or otherwise penalize requests. Keep model, precision, runtime, hardware, arrival process, and request mix fixed when evaluating it, and measure occupancy, queue time, TTFT, inter-token/end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, memory, and failures.
risks: Memory pressure can change admission behavior and invalidate simple throughput comparisons.
Averages can hide request starvation or tail-latency effects.
evidence_required: Scheduler and memory traces, admission/rejection events, batch occupancy, request-level latency/queue metrics, throughput, and failure/OOM counts.

source_user: Define continuous batching and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Continuous batching schedules a variable active set for each generation iteration, admitting eligible queued requests and retiring completed ones rather than waiting for a fixed batch's longest request. Mechanism: dynamic membership lets the runtime reuse compute capacity released by early finishers, which can improve utilization and goodput for heterogeneous lengths. Boundary: the result depends on iteration granularity, scheduler fairness, padding/packing, arrival rate, and KV-cache capacity; it may increase queueing or tail latency at saturation. Use matched static and continuous policies, warm up and repeat randomized trials, then report request-level latency percentiles, queue time, throughput/goodput, occupancy, memory, utilization, and errors.
risks: Goodput gains may be obtained by sacrificing fairness or tail latency.
Different packing and arrival processes can confound policy comparisons.
evidence_required: Identical workload and configuration manifests, iteration/batch traces, repeated request-level metrics, memory/utilization telemetry, and failure accounting.

source_user: Contrast continuous batching with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: A naive static-batch decoder holds one fixed request group until the group completes, so short requests can leave unused slots while a long request continues. Continuous batching instead refreshes membership at iteration boundaries: completed requests are retired and waiting requests can be admitted. Mechanism: this reuses freed active slots and can reduce idle capacity from output-length skew. Boundary: it is not a universal throughput or latency win; scheduler overhead, KV-cache capacity, admission limits, and queueing can dominate, and fairness may worsen. Compare both policies on identical arrival and length distributions, model/runtime settings, and load, reporting per-request TTFT, inter-token and tail latency, queue time, throughput/goodput, memory, and errors.
risks: The baseline may differ in kernels, padding, or request admission.
Aggregate tokens/s may hide starvation and p99 latency regressions.
evidence_required: Matched policy implementations, batch membership and queue traces, length/load sweep, request-level latency percentiles, throughput, memory, utilization, and failures.

source_user: Contrast continuous batching with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Without continuous batching, a static batch commonly keeps completed requests' slots reserved until the batch's remaining sequences finish, unless another explicit packing policy intervenes. Continuous batching changes the active set at decode iteration boundaries, removing finished requests and admitting queued ones. Mechanism: the replacement request can share subsequent decode iterations with survivors, reducing padding/idle work caused by length variation. Boundary: replacement is limited by scheduler timing and available KV memory; at low load or with equal lengths, the benefit may be negligible, while at saturation it can raise queue or tail latency. Use the same request stream and report batch traces, queue time, TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, memory, utilization, and failures.
risks: Static batching semantics vary, so an ill-defined baseline weakens attribution.
Memory contention can change both admission and latency distributions.
evidence_required: Explicit baseline/policy definitions, iteration-level membership traces, controlled repeated load tests, request-level latency tails, queueing, memory, and error data.
